cues.text: A sealed tomb in the Valley of the Kings.
A warning, it is said, guarded its door:

death would come swiftly
to anyone who disturbed the king.

And within five months
of the tomb's opening,

the man who had paid
for the search was dead.

This is the curse of Tutankhamun,
as it has been told for a hundred years.

But in the records we
checked, we could not find

that warning as an inscription
from the tomb.
So where did the curse come from?

In this episode, we follow the story
from a step in the sand, to the newspapers

of 1923, and back to tales of mummies
written long before the tomb was found.

On the fourth of November,
1922, Egyptian workmen digging

for the archaeologist Howard
Carter uncovered a step cut

into the rock, in the Valley
of the Kings, near Luxor.

Carter had the stairway
covered again, and sent

a telegram to his patron
in England, Lord Carnarvon.

On the twenty-sixth of November,
with Carnarvon beside him,

Carter made a small hole in a sealed
doorway and held up a candle.

Asked if he could see
anything, he answered,

as he later wrote in his book:
"Yes, wonderful things."
It was the tomb of a young king who had

ruled more than three
thousand years earlier.
Robbers had entered it in ancient times,

but many of the things buried
with him were still there.

On the sixteenth of February,
1923, before invited guests,

the sealed door of the burial
chamber was opened.

The discovery made
headlines around the world.

Lord Carnarvon placed
the reporting of the excavation

in the hands of one London
newspaper, The Times.

In the race for news, stories from outside
the tomb began to fill the papers too.

In March 1923, Carnarvon fell ill
with an infection, and then pneumonia.

On the fifth of April, he died
in Cairo, at the age of fifty-six.

Newspapers around the world
linked his death to the tomb.

They also reported
the novelist Marie Corelli's

belief in ancient powers
protecting the tomb.

The writer Arthur Conan Doyle
was quoted as suggesting

that a spirit-like force guarding
the tomb might be to blame.

On the same pages,
other experts disagreed.

The famous warning appeared
as the story was retold.

We have not found a reliable source
placing those words in the tomb itself.

Among the tomb's real texts are
wishes for the king's eternal life.

One alabaster cup carries a wish
for him to live for millions of years.

Stories of mummies
and the dangers of their tombs

were already being read
long before the discovery.

In 1869, Louisa May Alcott,
the author of Little Women,

published "Lost in a Pyramid;
or, The Mummy's Curse,"

a tale of seeds taken from a tomb
that bring misfortune.

In 1892, Conan Doyle
himself published "Lot No.

249," in which a mummy
is brought back to life.

Ancient Egypt did have
warnings of its own.

One tomb chapel from around
2400 BC, more than a thousand

years before Tutankhamun,
warns that anyone who enters it

unclean and does it harm will
be judged by the great god.
Those warnings are real.
They simply belong to other tombs.
And the people around the tomb?

The work of recording
and clearing it went on for about

ten years, and Howard
Carter lived until 1939.

In 2002, a study
in the British Medical Journal

looked at the Westerners
named in Carter's records.

It found no statistically
significant link between attending

the opening events defined
by the study and how long people lived.

It was a small study
with incomplete records.
So where did the curse come from?

The story grew around
older tales of mummies,

a sudden and tragic death,
and arguments in the newspapers.

The tomb itself held a young king,
and words wishing him eternal life.
Every story has an origin.

Sometimes, it begins
with a candle held up in the dark.

This video is based on historical
texts and public museum collections.

The narration uses synthetic speech,
and one scene uses AI-generated imagery.

Sources and terms of use are
listed in the description.
If you enjoyed this story, please like

the video and subscribe
for more quiet origins.
Thank you for watching.
